title: “Workers unite the world”: how BMS answered a famous slogan
author: Editorial Desk
summary: In the 1950s the popular call was ‘Workers of the world, unite!’. BMS turned the sentence around.
body:
In the 1950s, the slogan most often raised at labour gatherings was *“Workers of the world, unite!”* BMS saw in it a call for disruption and class hatred. Its answer was to turn the sentence around: **“Workers unite the world.”**

## Builders, not destroyers

The change is more than wordplay. In the first slogan, the worker's task is to fight a class enemy. In the second, the worker is a **builder**, whose labour has the power to bring a divided world together. Production, peace and cooperation come before conflict.

## A change you can hear

BMS's own story is that the older cry of *Inquilab Zindabad* at labour gatherings gradually made way for *Bharat Mata ki Jai*. That change tells how Indian labour found a voice that was its own.

## Not soft, but different

None of this means that BMS avoids struggle. It organises demonstrations, memoranda and, when needed, strikes. But it keeps a rule: demands must be firm, and methods must be constructive. *The Onward March of BMS* explains that BMS did not want a union that was merely agitational, and that as a nationalist organisation it should ensure that production is not hampered.

## The international angle

The slogan has had a second life at international forums. Representatives of BMS at the BRICS Trade Union Forum have spoken about worker-centric cooperation among nations, which is the same thought in a global setting.
